Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

vignette:
Linh is a 48-year-old Vietnamese-American woman who works as a waitress at a mid-sized family restaurant in her city. She is divorced and lives alone. She was referred for psychological assessment following a disclosure to her primary care physician, and she arrived at the intake appointment guarded, speaking quietly and rarely making eye contact.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Linh became aware that a man she had briefly dated was following her. What began as repeated appearances at her restaurant - sitting in her section, watching her move between tables - escalated over several months into notes left on her car, phone calls at 2 a.m., and on one occasion, the discovery that he had been standing outside her apartment building for hours. The stalking reached its peak on a night when she returned home from a closing shift to find her front door unlocked. She did not know whether he had been inside. She stood in the doorway for what she later described as a very long time, unable to move or speak. Police involvement eventually led to a restraining order, but by then the damage, as Linh understood it, was already done.

In the weeks that followed, something in Linh's memory of those months refused to settle into ordinary recollection. She finds that she cannot put what happened into coherent language - when she tries to describe the period to anyone, including her therapist, the words do not arrive in the right order, and what she produces feels disconnected from anything she recognises as herself. The memory, she says, feels like it belongs to a different woman entirely. And yet it does not stay at a distance: it forces itself into her mind without warning, most often when she is mid-task at work - carrying plates, taking an order - and the intrusion leaves her physically shaken, heart hammering, skin flushed. These unbidden returns of the experience feed directly into how she now understands her life: she has come to believe that the woman she was before - someone she remembers as genuinely happy, someone who found pleasure in small things - is simply gone. Nothing in her days feels meaningful. She describes herself as feeling dead inside, a phrase she returns to with a flatness that suggests it is not metaphor but diagnosis.

This profound sense of inner loss has in turn shaped how vigilantly she monitors the world around her. Because she has concluded that safety is no longer something she can take for granted, she listens for sounds at night - footsteps in the hallway, the particular creak of the building's entrance - and she avoids any place she has not been before, reasoning that unfamiliar environments offer no baseline against which to detect danger. At the restaurant, this plays out concretely: she has quietly arranged her sections so that she works only the tables nearest the kitchen, where she can see both the entrance and the back exit simultaneously. When a new customer sits in an unfamiliar part of the floor, she finds reasons to ask a colleague to cover. The hypervigilance is exhausting, and its exhaustion deepens her conviction that her life has become unrecognisable.

The sense of permanent diminishment and the constant state of alert together drive a set of strategies that have narrowed her world considerably. She avoids the friends she socialised with before the stalking began - seeing them, she fears, would require her to account for who she has become, and she cannot bear that reflection. Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation she sidesteps entirely, even minor ones at work, because conflict now registers in her body as threat. She has also begun to avoid looking at or touching her own body, as though it too is a site she no longer trusts. These withdrawals, over the months, have had the effect of sealing off the very contexts in which the memory might be processed or spoken - without social contact, without embodied presence, without the friction of ordinary disagreement, there is nothing to interrupt the memory's uncontrolled returns, and so it continues to arrive uninvited, sustaining the dread and the emptiness in equal measure.

What finally brought Linh to seek help was a shift at the restaurant last month in which she froze completely when a male customer raised his voice at a colleague near her station. She stood holding a tray, unable to move, until a coworker touched her arm. She is most afraid, she says, that this is simply who she is now. What she is hoping for, though she offers it tentatively, is to feel something again.
